title: Conveyor: gear motors, rollers, belts, sensors and 24 V supplies
summary: A conveyor line gives you gear motors and right-angle reducers, dozens of sealed-bearing rollers with their axles, belts, chains and sprockets, 24 V photo-eyes and power supplies, contactors and steel frames. Allow an hour or more per section. Lock out the power before you reach in: belts, rollers and chains pinch and pull hands in, and the sections are heavy.

steps.text: Walk the line and work out what you have: a powered belt with a drive and a tail roller, chain-driven live rollers, 24 V motor-driven rollers, or plain gravity rollers. Find the drive end, the control panel and the emergency stops. Clear anything off the belt and rollers.

Lock out the power at the panel isolator or breaker: switch it off, lock or tape it and leave a note. Isolate any separate control or 24 V supply and any other conveyor that feeds this one. Prove it dead at the motor's terminal box and in the panel (see safety_mains_isolation). Bleed the air from any pneumatic stop or gate.
steps.warn: A conveyor can restart by itself if someone switches it on or a sensor triggers. Hands near a belt or chain get pulled in. Lock out first.

steps.text: Stored energy: block any inclined section so it cannot roll back, and support raised sections on stands before you unbolt anything. If the line has a drive or inverter in the panel, wait 10 minutes after isolation, measure the DC bus and discharge any capacitor over 30 V (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
Take off the guards and covers: side guards, chain covers and belt covers. They are usually a few bolts or screws each, and the sheet metal is sharp.
steps.warn: Edges on guards and frames are sharp. Wear gloves.

steps.text: Belts: slacken the take-up (the adjusting bolts at the tail roller) fully, then cut the belt at its joint or unlace the fastener, and pull it out from one end. Fabric and PVC belts are 3–5 mm thick, so cut with a sharp knife or a hook blade. Roll the belt up for storage, or cut it into 1–2 m pieces.
steps.warn: Never reach into the gap between belt and pulley. Even slack, a belt can pull fingers in and a cut end can spring back.

steps.text: Chains: find the master link (the one with a clip), remove the clip with pliers and take the link out. Coil the chain with its oil. Sprockets are held by set screws or keys: undo the set screw and pull each off its shaft.

Drive: label the motor wires at the terminal box with tape (photograph the terminal layout) and disconnect them. Support the gear motor with a block or a helper, undo the mounting bolts and slide it off its shaft or coupling. Gear motors with reducers weigh 15–40 kg.
steps.warn: A gear motor drops hard once the last bolt is out. Support it before you undo that bolt.

steps.text: Rollers: each roller sits between the side frames on a spring-loaded hex axle or is held by bolts. For spring axles, push the axle end in with a screwdriver, tilt the roller and lift it out. Keep each roller with its own axle and sort by diameter and length.
steps.warn: Spring-loaded axles snap back and pinch fingers between roller and frame. Keep your fingers out of the gap.

steps.text: Motor-driven rollers: unplug the roller's connector or cut its cable 15 cm from the roller. Keep the roller whole, together with the control card for its zone if there is one. The motor is inside the tube.
Sensors and stops: unscrew the photo-eyes and their reflectors from the frame and cut the cables 20 cm back. Unscrew the emergency stop buttons and pull cords.

Control panel: after you have proved the supply dead again, unwire the 24 V power supplies, contactors, overload relays and terminal blocks from their rails, labelling the wires. Take photographs of the layout first.
Frames last: unbolt the side frames from the legs and cross-members, working from the free end to the fixed end. A 3 m section can weigh 40–100 kg: use two people and keep it level.
steps.warn: Frames can fall or twist as the last bolts come out. Support each end before you undo them.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Gear motors.** AC gear motors of 0.25–2 kW, single or three-phase, and right-angle reducers. Read the nameplate for the voltage, phase and speed (see skill_read_nameplate and test_motor). Worm reducers can't be turned backwards by their load, so they make good winch and hoist drives but poor generators.
- **Motor rollers.** Roller conveyors with zone control use 24 V brushless motors inside the roller tube. They need the zone card or a brushless controller that reads their Hall sensors. Check the wiring and test with a 24 V supply before you plan on them.
- **Rollers and axles.** Dozens of steel or plastic rollers on sealed ball bearings: use as axles, wheels, a roller table, a rope guide or a sliding rack. Their bearings are small sealed deep-groove types: read the number on the face.
- **Belts.** PVC or rubber belts make a conveyor again, a mat, gaskets, strap or a belt-drive.
- **Chains and sprockets.** Standard roller chain: gear drives, a winch or a bicycle-style drive.
- **Photo-eyes and reflectors.** 24 V sensors: build a perimeter alarm or counter (see build_perimeter_alarm).
- **24 V supplies.** Compact DIN-rail 24 V DC supplies: they power sensors, locks and LED lights from mains.
- **Contactors and relays.** Motor starters rated 9–40 A, with 24 V, 120 V or 230 V coils. Check the coil voltage on the label.
- **Frames.** Steel or aluminium side frames and legs: rack, bench, cart or shelf stock.
- **Emergency stops.** Large red mushroom buttons, handy as a master kill switch.

## Variations

- Supermarket checkout belts hold a small gear motor, a belt and a photo-eye each. They come out in about 20 minutes.
- Airport baggage lines use heavy belts and curves with chains: stay out of the pits.
- Pallet and heavy-duty conveyors use thick chains and much larger motors: use lifting gear and more helpers.
- Plastic modular belts are made of interlocking links that unclip with a rod.

## What to leave

- Anything bolted to a concrete floor that you can't lift out.
- Drive units or hoppers that are still under load.
- Pneumatic stops and diverters unless you have vented them.
